qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

As part of its health watch, the French National Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health and Safety (ANSES) is once again alerting the public to ‘cases of adverse effects’ caused by food supplements for athletes, particularly bodybuilders1. In France, between 2016 and February 2024, 154 new cases of adverse effects were reported, of which 18 were considered very serious. Two deaths were reported and four people suffered life-threatening symptoms. Some of these food supplements contain banned and dangerous substances, such as anabolic steroids or sibutramine, banned in France since 20102. These components can lead to cardiovascular complications. Moreover, labels do not always indicate the presence of such substances in a given food supplement. ANSES recommends avoiding purchasing these food supplements on the internet. Customs controls, which have become virtually non-existent, make it impossible to detect prohibited and dangerous substances contained in these products, which are often imported. 1.
Is the Commission aware of these cases of fraud concerning food supplements?
Is the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) carrying out risk assessments of these products, including of their cocktail effects?
Is the Commission considering amending the legislation in place to address this problem?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.9.2024) The Commission is aware of fraud cases concerning food supplements as reported by the Honourable Member. In fact, more than 1,000 non-compliances on food supplements were reported by Member States’ authorities within the EU Alert and Cooperation Network (ACN)1 between January 2023 and July 2024, amongst which two-thirds were reported within the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed. Out of these, 78 cases relate to the presence of unauthorised substances (such as medicines, stimulants, and doping substances) and 392 to the detection of ingredients that are not authorised in the EU. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) performs comprehensive risk assessments on the safety of substances used in food supplements before any EU authorisation is granted. The presence of medicines, stimulants, and doping substances in food and of substances unauthorised as food ingredients, are in breach with EU legislation. While the current EU legal framework is considered to be fit for purpose, its implementation and enforcement remain under the responsibility of the Member States. The Commission will continue assisting Member States in these responsibilities, notably through EU coordinated actions2 and enhancing communication and cooperation through its ACN. The European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) also supports Member States in preventing and combating organised fraud in the sector3.
